tier_reason: The blog post (read from its Markdown source in the Quuxplusone/blog repo, since the github.io page is blocked) gives first-party numbers against std::mt19937: half the generation speed, 500x slower seeding, and an all-2^32-seeds loop of about 90 minutes vs eight seconds; the machine is unnamed and the QuickBench code it links is on an egress-blocked host, so it falls short of A and has no independent measurement for B.

corrections.workload: Blog post 'Underseeding mt19937; introducing xoshiro256ss' (2021-11-23): exhaustive loop seeding the engine with every 32-bit value and drawing one output, std::mt19937 vs xoshiro256ss; QuickBench of seeding cost (libc++ and libstdc++ links, std::default_random_engine also included); a separate QuickBench of output generation.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Post TLDR: 'std::mt19937 is half the speed of a good PRNG (and 500 times slower to seed)'. Exhaustive seed loop: std::mt19937 constructed from a 32-bit seed takes about 1.2 microseconds per iteration, so all 4.3 billion seeds take about 90 minutes; with xoshiro256ss the same loop takes about eight seconds (about 675x, derived from page data). Seeding QuickBench: xoshiro256ss 'several hundred times faster' to seed than mt19937 and '50% faster than' std::default_random_engine; generation QuickBench: 'markedly faster at generating output' (no number printed in the post). The repo README says only 'speedily'.
corrections.caveats: Port only: the author says he translated Blackman and Vigna's xoshiro256** and splitmix64 C code to C++ (about 50 lines) with the <random> engine interface, and the repo's test vectors check it matches the reference C code; the speed advantage belongs to the xoshiro256** algorithm, already catalogued as https://prng.di.unimi.it. Numbers are first-party, from an unnamed machine and compiler; the libc++/libstdc++ split applies to the seeding QuickBench only, whose pages (quick-bench.com) were egress-blocked here, so the QuickBench timings were not read. The post itself warns it emphasizes seeding, which a good program does once, over generation. No LICENSE file; 'Public domain' is stated only in the README (no patent grant). Single commit from 2021-05-13, over 5 years old.

notes: Port/wrapper only: Xoshiro256ss is a 50-line C-to-C++ translation of the reference xoshiro256** with no algorithmic change; its measured advantage over std::mt19937 is the algorithm's, not the port's. Suggest decision 'duplicate' of https://prng.di.unimi.it (precedent ademakov/rng). The post was read via https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Quuxplusone/blog/master/_posts/2021-11-23-xoshiro.md, the source of the github.io page. Tried quick-bench.com/q/zopXiKjSDnta4Uz3t88Dp2O7OH0: EGRESS_BLOCKED.

tier_reason: The README's Performance section claims the code is 'faster than any other published method' and that the paper's Listing 2 would be about 3x faster, but it names no baseline and gives no timings; generate_samples.cpp prints its own wall time but no results are published, so D.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'I don't think there are any faster or simpler open-source implementations out there' and 'the code in this library is faster than any other published method'; no timings and no named baseline. It also says the minimal 2D Sobol' code of Listing 2 in the paper would be about 3x faster than this general-purpose code. Paper abstract (WebSearch snippet only, not read): an Owen-scrambled Sobol' (0,2)-sequence implementation in fewer than 30 lines of C++ generates 200 million samples per second on a single CPU thread; the snippet gives no baseline figure.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 55 stars, 2 forks, 18 commits; reference implementation by the first author of the EGSR 2021 paper (DOI 10.2312/sr.20211287)
corrections.caveats: Claim has no comparative numbers and no named baseline. The paper (diglib.eg.org) and the co-author's abstract page (seanet.com) are egress-blocked here, so whether the paper times other Owen-scrambling or pmj02 generators is unknown; a paper-access retier could lift it to B. generate_samples.cpp times its own run (std::chrono) but nothing is published. Quasi-random generators have no mt19937/PCG/xoshiro equivalent, so baseline_in_list is false. The 2026 commits only edit the README; the last code change is the 2023-12-14 merge of a 32-bit PR.
